pages.text:
The File menu opened, with Save (+ export sheets) marked 1
① Save (+ export sheets) in the File menu — Ctrl+S
The status bar after saving, with the message about the saved file and exported sheet marked 2
② The status bar after saving: the saved .chickxel and the exported sheet and cell count
Ctrl+S (① File > Save (+ export sheets)) saves the .chickxel, also exports the images and meta files if export is on, and ② shows the result in the status bar. When there is nothing to save, the toolbar's save button is disabled.
What a save does
The project is written in full to a temporary file in the same folder (….chickxel-tmp), which then replaces the original .chickxel.
If Export on save is on in the export dialog (the default for new projects), the frame sheet, part atlas, meta files and .spriteLib are written (where outputs go). If it is off, the status bar adds (export off).
Old outputs exported last time but not produced this time are moved to the app trash (Cleaning up old outputs).
The status bar shows Saved: file name with the exported sheet names and cell counts (plus + .meta if meta files were written), and the file is added to recent files and undo history.
When meta files are written
The meta file next to each image (.meta) is written according to Write .meta in the export dialog.
Setting Meta file
Auto (default) Written only when the image is inside a Unity project's Assets folder or already has a .meta.
Always Always written.
Off Not written. However, with Sprite Library on, the part atlas meta file is always written (the library must point to its sprites), and .spriteLib files always get a meta file too.
When rewriting an existing meta file, its guid and each sprite's spriteID are kept. Sprites with the same cell name keep their IDs, and a renamed cell inherits the ID of the old cell at the same position, so references on the Unity side don't break.
The name on first save
The first time you save a never-saved new project (Save or Save as), the save dialog suggests its temporary title as the name (without characters not allowed in file names; sprite if nothing is left or there is no temporary title). If that name already exists in the folder the dialog opens in (the file browser's current folder, otherwise the last folder), the first free name such as sprite_1.chickxel, sprite_2.chickxel… is used.
Save as
Ctrl+Shift+S (File > Save as…) saves to a location and name you pick, and the current document then points to that new file. It doesn't make a separate copy, so later saves go to the new file. The original file and the outputs exported under its name stay where they are and aren't cleaned up. Outputs that used the default name are created under the new project name; a folder or name set explicitly in the export dialog is kept as is.
Exporting without saving
The Export button in the export dialog (Ctrl+E) writes only the outputs with the current settings, without saving the .chickxel (a never-saved document asks for a save location first). Old outputs are cleaned up the same way as on save. GIFs are made separately with Export as animated GIF.
If saving fails
The Save failed dialog, with the message that the project was saved but the sheet export failed marked 3
③ The project was saved but exporting the sheet/.meta failed (Save failed)
If the .chickxel was saved but only exporting the outputs failed (for example because another program has an image open), ③ you're told about it. The project counts as saved.
Message Meaning and what to do
Couldn't save The .chickxel couldn't be written. The document stays modified; remove the cause and save again, or save under another name.
The file is read-only Turn off read-only in the file's properties, or save under another name.
Another program has the file open Close that program (image viewer, game engine, sync app, …) or save under another name.
Export file names collide The project is saved and only the export fails. Rename the frame sheet, part atlas, tag, part or skin so they differ.
When saving takes a while
If saving or opening a project takes a while, a dark translucent overlay covers the whole window until it finishes. A box in the middle shows Saving or Opening, a spinning loading icon, the percentage with a progress bar and Editing is paused until this finishes. Meanwhile drawing, shortcuts and file drops are ignored and other windows (such as the AI chat) are disabled; AI tool calls run once it finishes. Closing the window then closes it after the save completes.

pages.text:
AI-generated "pixel-look" images have uneven pixel sizes (e.g. 7–9 px), blurred edges, JPEG noise and hundreds of colors. The Pixelate AI image window turns such an image into clean pixel art in which each source cell becomes one result pixel. The source can have a solid or transparent background, and can be a sprite sheet with several frames or an animated GIF.
An AI-made source next to the pixelated result
Left: AI-made source (7–8 px cells, blur and JPEG noise) · Right: 49×98 result from the Default preset (enlarged 4×)
Workflow
When the window gets a source, it lays out one candidate tile per checked preset, and Clean up or Auto optimize fills them with results. Usually you compare the candidates, pick one and apply it; you only change settings when no result looks right.
Load a source: open the window and drop or paste an image. Each checked preset gets a candidate tile; run them with Clean up or Auto optimize.
Compare candidates: click candidate tiles to see the large preview and score, and compare with the source cell by cell in the enlarged view.
Find better settings (when needed): run Auto optimize, or change values in the pipeline steps and press Clean up.
Touch up colors (when needed): remove unwanted colors from the chosen result, or pick a missing color from the source and pin it.
Insert: press Apply or Add to new tab to insert the result as a new layer in the current document or as a new document.
How the conversion works
Each result goes through the steps below in order. What each step does and when to change it is summarized in the table on Pipeline settings.
Step What it does
Remove background · Split frames Makes the background transparent and splits a sheet into frames.
Pixel grid · Output size Finds how many source pixels make one "pixel" (the cell size) and where the cell boundaries are, then decides the output size.
Cell color · Palette Picks one representative color per cell and merges similar colors into a palette.
Cleanup · Frame consistency Fixes orphan pixels and holes, fits the outline to 1 px, and reduces flicker between frames.
Score Rates each result from 0 to 100 (similarity to the source, clean outlines and more) so candidates can be compared.

Uses a straight grid with the cell size and start X/Y you set (see the manual grid table below). Choose it when Auto finds double or half the real cell size, or when you know the scale the pixel art was enlarged by. On AI images with uneven cells a straight grid tends to drift off the edges in places.

Uses block edges when the block spacing is clear; otherwise fits cell lines for each of the three values and picks the one that best matches the source's strong edges. The match subtracts what the same edges would match by chance if shuffled (bigger cells match more by chance). On a near tie the order is outline → block edges → color edges, and a value 2× or 3× the pick wins if it matches almost as well.
Measures the dark band touching transparency in several places horizontally and vertically, and picks the size that makes the outline 1 px.
Estimates the cell size as a decimal from run lengths between color changes; tolerant to jitter, preferring the finer of two harmonics.

Ignoring weak texture such as paper grain (only where neighboring pixels differ by more than the image's noise in OKLab), picks the spacing at which strong color edges line up within a row. It prefers the larger cell even with half-cell blocks mixed in, and places the cell lines on those strong edges.

blocks.alt: Local cell correction in the 3. Pixel grid step

runs.t: ③ Local cell correction, Max shift, Band, Minimum cell size

(on by default) re-fits the image-wide cell lines per band to that band's strong block edges. It follows art that is drawn half a cell off in places; within a band the lines stay straight so cells are rectangles, and the lines bend where bands change.

rows.t: Maximum distance a line may move from its image-wide position. Neighboring cell widths stay within 70–130% of the original, so actual movement can be smaller.
Width of each band fitted separately. Smaller follows more closely (1 = every row), larger is smoother.
The average cell size (in source pixels) from which correction applies. Lower values also adjust small cells but may follow blurred-edge noise.

runs.t: Each band counts color edges that continue over several rows, drops 1–2 px noise, and weights high-contrast edges more, so sharp continuous edges are matched first. Two sharp edges within one cell (e.g. two black-to-skin edges 5 px apart) can't both be matched by one line.

Even when on, the grid stays straight if the average cell is below the minimum or no line moved. The selected-result line shows whether it applied, such as "Local correction applied to n/m frames". With step 3's
on, Clean up and Auto optimize also try it on and off with different max shift and band values.
decides how many pixels the result has.

rows.t: Each detected cell becomes one result pixel (default). It keeps the pixel count the source art was drawn at, so it is the most faithful choice when no size is required.

. The source sprite is divided into the cell count left after padding: at 64×64 with padding 1, the cell size is chosen so the long side has 62 cells, splitting or merging cells. Multiplies the source size by a factor (e.g. 0.125), using the cell lines found per frame. Use it when you know the enlargement (0.125 for 8×) or want several images reduced by the same ratio.

The cell split score looks only at the source and the cell lines: the average of Cell edge fit (higher when the lines miss none of the source's strong edges and lie on them — cells smaller or larger than the real ones both score low) and Cell color purity (higher when each cell holds only similar colors). Add to auto pixel size (px) and the manual grid's start X/Y depend on the image, so Clean up uses them but they aren't saved in presets or for the next session (changing only them doesn't turn the save button red).
Local cell correction
Local cell correction in the 3. Pixel grid step
③ Local cell correction, Max shift, Band, Minimum cell size
③ Local cell correction (on by default) re-fits the image-wide cell lines per band to that band's strong block edges. It follows art that is drawn half a cell off in places; within a band the lines stay straight so cells are rectangles, and the lines bend where bands change.
Setting Range · default Meaning
Max shift (% of cell) 5–99%, default 35% Maximum distance a line may move from its image-wide position. Neighboring cell widths stay within 70–130% of the original, so actual movement can be smaller.
Band (cells) 1–32 cells, default 2 Width of each band fitted separately. Smaller follows more closely (1 = every row), larger is smoother.
Minimum cell size (px) 1–16 px, default 4 px The average cell size (in source pixels) from which correction applies. Lower values also adjust small cells but may follow blurred-edge noise.
Each band counts color edges that continue over several rows, drops 1–2 px noise, and weights high-contrast edges more, so sharp continuous edges are matched first. Two sharp edges within one cell (e.g. two black-to-skin edges 5 px apart) can't both be matched by one line.
Even when on, the grid stays straight if the average cell is below the minimum or no line moved. The selected-result line shows whether it applied, such as "Local correction applied to n/m frames". With step 3's Optimize on, Clean up and Auto optimize also try it on and off with different max shift and band values.
4. Output size
② 4. Output size decides how many pixels the result has. Auto next to the mode is the same setting as the output size Auto in Quick settings (off = fit a fixed size, on = the last automatic mode).
Mode Output size
From pixel size Each detected cell becomes one result pixel (default). It keeps the pixel count the source art was drawn at, so it is the most faithful choice when no size is required.
Fit a fixed size Fits Width×Height (e.g. 32, 48, 64), with Keep aspect and Padding (px). The source sprite is divided into the cell count left after padding: at 64×64 with padding 1, the cell size is chosen so the long side has 62 cells, splitting or merging cells. If the detected cell size is within 2% of that, the detected lines are kept; cells are never smaller than one source pixel. Use it when the game needs a set size, such as a 32×32 character.
Scale factor Multiplies the source size by a factor (e.g. 0.125), using the cell lines found per frame. Use it when you know the enlargement (0.125 for 8×) or want several images reduced by the same ratio.

runs.t: From left: source gradients (top to bottom apricot, gold, red, blue, grey, green; lighter on the left) · OKLab · CIEDE2000 · OKLCh hue-weighted (default) — same 10-color palette, Prefer shade family off.

OKLab weighs lightness, chroma and hue equally, so the middle of the grey strip turns skin and apricot, dark gold turns green and red, and dark ends go navy instead of black. CIEDE2000 keeps the greys cleanly grey, navy and black and holds gold almost to the dark end; OKLCh hue-weighted counts hue differences double, so greys stay in the grey family and gold shading stays among warm colors (apricot, red). Pictures with many greys, metals or dark shading do better with CIEDE2000 or OKLCh hue-weighted; for evenly spread colors OKLab is enough.

rows.t: Default. Splits the OKLab difference into lightness (L), chroma (C, how intense a color is) and hue (H, which color it is: red, yellow, blue and so on), and counts only the hue part more, by the hue weight next to it (default 2). A palette color of the same hue therefore wins even if its lightness is a bit off, so deep apricot hand shading doesn't turn into a gold or red-cloth color of similar lightness. The hue difference is scaled by chroma, so greys, whites and blacks are barely affected. Suits characters where different hues of similar lightness sit side by side, such as skin, hair and clothes.

The industry-standard color difference formula (ΔE00) used in print and displays, measured in CIELAB (divided by 200 to match the OKLab scale). Differences the eye is dull to (chroma between very saturated colors) count less, sensitive ones (between near-grey colors) count more, and a correction for hue shifts around blue and purple is built in. It separates the fine steps of silver armor or white clothes and the shading of blue clothes well, and doesn't treat a hue change (apricot → gold) as close. It is heavier to compute, so cleanup gets a little slower.

built so that colors the same number apart look about equally different (perceptually uniform: around 0.02 is a barely visible difference whether the colors are dark or light, red or blue). This takes the straight (Euclidean) distance between two colors in it, weighing lightness, chroma and hue equally (the old behavior). Fastest and most predictable, but at the same distance it can't tell one shading step from a neighboring hue, so shading can slip into the next hue. Suits images with few, clearly different colors.

Method Color picked

Median The per-channel median. Red, green and blue each take their middle value, so a few stray noise pixels don't move it; but since the channels are picked separately, a cell split half-and-half between two colors can get a color that isn't in the source.

Mean The mean; cells on an edge can get an in-between mix of two colors. Natural for soft gradients, but it tends to leave muddy in-between dots between outline and fill (see the figure below).
Center-weighted mean A mean that counts pixels near the cell center more (transparent pixels left out). Less affected by edge blur than Mean, but a cell whose middle an edge crosses still gets a mixed color.

Color snap step How far apart (in RGB channel units, default 20) colors can be and still count as one color for Most frequent color and Dominant-color weighted mean. Larger values gather a fill with JPEG noise into one color; too large merges two close shading steps. Other methods don't use it.

Color distance
③ Color distance is how closeness between two colors is measured. It is used when cells take a palette color (without dithering), for pinned colors, for the replacement of excluded colors, for picking original colors and by Distance grouping. The score uses a separate scoring color distance.

OKLab weighs lightness, chroma and hue equally, so the middle of the grey strip turns skin and apricot, dark gold turns green and red, and dark ends go navy instead of black. CIEDE2000 keeps the greys cleanly grey, navy and black and holds gold almost to the dark end; OKLCh hue-weighted counts hue differences double, so greys stay in the grey family and gold shading stays among warm colors (apricot, red). Pictures with many greys, metals or dark shading do better with CIEDE2000 or OKLCh hue-weighted; for evenly spread colors OKLab is enough.
Distance Character
OKLCh hue-weighted Default. Splits the OKLab difference into lightness (L), chroma (C, how intense a color is) and hue (H, which color it is: red, yellow, blue and so on), and counts only the hue part more, by the hue weight next to it (default 2). A palette color of the same hue therefore wins even if its lightness is a bit off, so deep apricot hand shading doesn't turn into a gold or red-cloth color of similar lightness. The hue difference is scaled by chroma, so greys, whites and blacks are barely affected. Suits characters where different hues of similar lightness sit side by side, such as skin, hair and clothes.
CIEDE2000 The industry-standard color difference formula (ΔE00) used in print and displays, measured in CIELAB (divided by 200 to match the OKLab scale). Differences the eye is dull to (chroma between very saturated colors) count less, sensitive ones (between near-grey colors) count more, and a correction for hue shifts around blue and purple is built in. It separates the fine steps of silver armor or white clothes and the shading of blue clothes well, and doesn't treat a hue change (apricot → gold) as close. It is heavier to compute, so cleanup gets a little slower.
OKLab OKLab is a color space built so that colors the same number apart look about equally different (perceptually uniform: around 0.02 is a barely visible difference whether the colors are dark or light, red or blue). This takes the straight (Euclidean) distance between two colors in it, weighing lightness, chroma and hue equally (the old behavior). Fastest and most predictable, but at the same distance it can't tell one shading step from a neighboring hue, so shading can slip into the next hue. Suits images with few, clearly different colors.
Hue weight (number box next to it) The factor on hue differences for OKLCh hue-weighted (0–1000, default 2). 0 ignores hue, 1 equals OKLab, 2–5 prefer the same hue family, and a very large value picks the closest hue regardless of lightness and chroma. Other distances don't use it.
k-means and OKLCH grouping always use OKLab, and Bayer dithering compares the light-linear mix of two palette colors with the source in OKLab.
Keeping shades and hues
④ Prefer shade family (on by default): if a palette color has a similar hue and chroma to the cell color (a lighter or darker shade of the same color), the cell takes the family member with the nearest lightness instead of a different-hue color of similar lightness. Dithering never mixes in a chromatic color of a different hue either, so deep apricot hand shading doesn't turn gold or get gold dots.
Keep distinct hues (on by default): if a source color group with enough chroma (Min chroma, default 0.04) and area (Min area, default 4 cells) would turn into a palette color whose hue differs by at least Hue diff (°) (default 20°) — e.g. small apricot ear shading → gold — that color is put in the palette: added with an automatic count, or swapped for the least important color with a fixed count (up to ¼ of the palette; pinned colors stay). Blurred in-between colors between two palette colors aren't added.
Optimizing the Palette step tries both on and off.
Dithering
Dither is None (default) · Bayer 2×2 · Bayer 4×4; a checker pattern of two palette colors makes the color in between (the same patterns as Converting colors to a palette). A pattern is used only when the mix is closer to the source than the single nearest color even after adding how noticeable the pattern is, and colors within a barely visible difference (OKLab 0.02) of a palette color aren't dithered.

Bayer 2×2 Makes a color missing from the palette with a 2×2 pattern of two palette colors (5 mixing levels). The tight pattern is less distracting on small sprites, but there are few in-between steps.
Bayer 4×4 The same with a 4×4 pattern (17 mixing levels). Wide gradients such as skies, glows and rounded shading blend more smoothly with a retro-console feel, but on small sprites the pattern can look like noise.
Don't optimize next to dithering (on by default) keeps optimization from changing it: a dither pattern's average color is close to the source, so it tends to raise the score even though zooming in shows a checkerboard or stray colored dots.

blocks.alt: 7. Cleanup with the Fit outline to 1 px list open

runs.t: ① 7. Cleanup · ② Fit outline to 1 px list
The items turned on in ①
apply in the order of the table below (orphans → holes → outline thinning → outline → L corners); Redraw as vector draws its new line before all of them.

rows.t: A pixel with no same-colored pixel among its 8 neighbors takes the most common neighbor color. Dots that contrast more than Max contrast (OKLab distance) with their neighbors, such as pupils, are kept; 1 removes them all.
Fills a transparent pixel painted on all four sides with the most common of those four colors.
How the outer outline is made 1 px; see the table below.

Used only by Redraw as vector. Simplify is how far (in result pixels) the outline may be straightened — larger is smoother but follows the shape less, 0 follows the center line exactly; dark shapes not touching the outer outline that are smaller than this many cells (such as eyes) are left as they are.
How the dark pixels on the edge (touching transparency) are tidied. What each value does is in the table below.
Replaces doubled pixels at L-shaped outline corners with the inner color.

blocks.alt: Legs of an image whose outline varies in color and is missing on the right leg, cleaned up with Outline As is, Unify to the darkest color and Ensure a closed 1-px outline, enlarged side by side

runs.t: From left: As is (default) · Unify to the darkest color · Ensure a closed 1-px outline — on a source whose outline is a different dark color per fill and missing on the right leg.

pages.title: Score and optimize criteria

runs.t: The score on each candidate (0–100) is computed without AI as a weighted sum of score terms. Clean up and
look for the settings with the highest score. The scoring rules and optimization budget are set per preset in
, and each candidate is scored by the criteria of the preset that made it.

rows.t: How closely the result matches the background-removed source cells: (opacity mismatches + structure loss inside cells + color difference) ÷ samples. Structure loss is how far the source pixels inside a cell scatter from the cell average — large in cells that cut a sharp edge in half, regardless of the result color. A higher weight favors results that follow the source's colors and shapes more closely (smaller cells, more colors); a lower one favors simpler results.

Share of orphan pixels with no same-colored pixel among their 8 neighbors (worst at 5% of opaque pixels). A higher weight favors clean results without specks, but penalizes art with many deliberate single dots such as pupils or sparkles.
Share of edge pixels that aren't outline (dark) colors. A higher weight favors results with an unbroken outline; set it to 0 for art drawn without outlines.
How far the color count is from the target. Unlike the others, it multiplies the whole score down (see Target colors below). With the target color count on Auto this weight does nothing.
How differently colors are used between frames. Nothing to measure with a single frame; in an animation a higher weight favors results whose colors flicker less from frame to frame.

How much the grid disagrees with color changes. The closer the cell lines sit between the source's color blocks, the better; a higher weight favors results whose cell size and lines match the source exactly.

Share of outer outline pixels that are only 1 px thick; doubled bands of 2 px or more count against it. Measured on the final placed pixels at outline darkness 0.24 even if you lower it, so leaving black outlines uncounted earns nothing. 1-px lines running inward from the outline aren't doubling. Lower it if a thick outline is part of the style.
How much a widely used source color (at least 1% of opaque pixels) turned into a different color as a whole (e.g. brown boots pulled toward gold). Measured with the scoring
(on the OKLab scale): up to 0.02 is fine; 0.10 is the worst. A higher weight favors results where large areas such as hair, clothes and boots keep their original hue.

How much the result is still an enlarged image: the share of edge cells (judged by each cell's average source color) that sit in a same-color 2×2 block. Close to 1 when cells are half the real size or smaller and the result is needlessly large;
can't hide it. Up to 65% is fine; 95% is the worst. Lowering it penalizes results cut finer (larger) than the source cells less.

runs.t: box decides how Fidelity compares result pixels with the source. The same result can lose or keep points for dither patterns or stray dots inside an outline depending on this value. It is a scoring rule, so optimization never changes it.

rows.t: Compares each result pixel with just its own source cell's color (see Representative cell color below) using the scoring color distance (default). Nothing is mixed with neighbors, so a stray colored dot inside an outline or a checkerboard dither pattern loses points cell by cell.
Ordinary pixel-art characters where clean fills and outlines matter, and every cell must match its own source cell.

Converts the source cell averages and the result into light-linear lightness, red–green and blue–yellow channels, blurs lightness a little and color more with neighboring cells, and compares in OKLab (S-CIELAB style; always OKLab instead of the scoring distance). A dither pattern that blends into the source color from a distance counts as a match.
Art that builds gradients with dithering, or has wide smooth areas such as skies and backgrounds; also for judging dithered results fairly.

When on (default), pixels near the cell center weigh more when choosing the cell color (a pyramid that falls off toward the edges). Neighbor colors bleeding over the cell edge count less, so the cell color stays steady even when the source cells are slightly uneven. Off counts every pixel in the cell equally.
Can be turned off for clean sources with little blur and exact cell edges.

runs.t: box decides which single color a source cell counts as when comparing cell by cell. Source cells mix in blur, noise and neighboring fills, so the same result scores differently depending on what is taken as the cell's color. Used only with

blocks.alt: Six source cells that mix colors next to the same cells filled with their dominant-group and cell-average reference colors

runs.t: From left: source cells (white lines = cell borders) · Dominant group (default) · Cell average — Cell average treats a cell that straddles two colors as a muddy in-between color that isn't in the source.
The cell split between outline and

and the cell with outline bled into a corner become skin with Dominant group but a muddy brown with Cell average. So Dominant group accepts a result that paints that cell plain skin, while Cell average rewards a result that paints the muddy brown that isn't in the source. The plain skin cell is the same in both, so the choice only changes the score on cells that mix colors.

rows.t: Groups similar colors in the cell (within the group range) and takes the heaviest group's average (default). A few black outline pixels in the corner of a skin cell, or blurred edge colors, form small groups and drop out, so a result that paints the cell clean skin color counts as a match.
Most AI pixel art with distinct outlines and fills.
Takes the average of every pixel in the cell. A cell an outline crosses gets a muddy mix of skin and black as its reference, so the result loses a little whether it paints that cell skin or black.
Soft painting where colors really blend inside each cell (gradients, watercolor style), so no single group stands out.

How different two colors can be and still form one group in Dominant group (OKLab distance, default 0.06). Smaller values split a single skin tone with JPEG noise into several groups, so the cell color wavers; larger values merge different fills such as skin and light shading. Optimize grid fit first's cell purity uses this value too.
Raise it a little for noisy JPEGs; lower it a little for art with closely spaced shading steps.

runs.t: A color distance is a ruler that turns how different two colors are into one number. The scoring color distance is used only for cell-by-cell Fidelity and Major color shift and never changes the result colors; it decides which differences count as worse mistakes among the same candidates. All three are on the OKLab scale, so the same thresholds apply (0.02 barely visible, 0.10 worst).

blocks.alt: Three color strips from one skin color, changing only lightness, only chroma and only hue

runs.t: From the top: lightness (L) — dark brown to pale skin · chroma (C) — grey to deep orange · hue (H) — one turn through the kinds of color at the same lightness and chroma. Each strip changes only that axis of one skin color.

OKLab and OKLCh are color spaces built so that differences match what the eye sees. OKLab places a color at lightness L and two color axes, a (green ↔ red) and b (blue ↔ yellow), and measures the difference as the straight distance between two points. OKLCh writes the same color as lightness L, chroma C (how vivid) and hue H (the kind of color), so you can see along which axis and how far a color moved, like the three strips above. The L·C·H weights of
multiply the differences on these three axes — raising H counts a change of kind of color (third strip) as bigger than a change of lightness only (first strip).

blocks.alt: Apricot, gold, red, blue, grey and green gradients mapped to one 10-color palette with three color distances

runs.t: From left: source gradients (top to bottom apricot, gold, red, blue, grey, green; lighter on the left) · OKLab · CIEDE2000 · OKLCh hue-weighted (default) — each pixel replaced by the nearest of the same 10 palette colors.

The scoring color distance measures the color difference between source and result with the same yardstick that picks the "nearest color" in this picture. Under OKLab, apricot in the middle of the grey strip and green where dark gold was count as close, so such a result loses little score; under CIEDE2000 and OKLCh hue-weighted they are a change to another color and are penalized heavily. So for pictures with many greys, metals or shadows, or where kinds of color must not mix, scoring with CIEDE2000 or OKLCh hue-weighted is safer (the distance that picks palette colors is set separately by the color distance in

rows.t: built so that colors the same number apart look about equally different (perceptually uniform: around 0.02 is a barely visible difference whether the colors are dark or light, red or blue). This takes the straight (Euclidean) distance in it, weighing lightness, chroma and hue equally. Fastest and simplest.
Images with few, clearly different colors, or when you want a neutral ruler that weighs no difference specially.

The industry-standard color difference formula (ΔE00) used in print and displays, measured in CIELAB (divided by 200 to match the OKLab scale). Differences the eye is dull to (chroma between very saturated colors) count less, sensitive ones (between near-grey colors) count more, and a correction for hue shifts around blue and purple is built in. Heavier to compute, so scoring gets a little slower.
Art with many grey steps such as silver armor, grey stone or white clothes, or with lots of blue such as blue clothes or a night sky.

Splits the OKLab difference into lightness (L), chroma (C, intensity) and hue (H, which color: red, yellow, blue and so on) and adds them with the L, C and H weights below (default 1 · 1 · 2, so hue counts double). The hue difference is scaled by chroma, so greys barely change and only a saturated color turning into another hue is penalized heavily. For example, a skin-colored hand turning red-cloth colored counts as a big mistake even at similar lightness.
Characters where different hues of similar lightness touch, such as skin, a red shirt and orange hair; for weeding out results whose shading slips into a neighboring hue.

The factor on chroma differences (default 1). Raising it penalizes colors that faded (vivid red → dull red) or grew more intense; 0 ignores chroma.
Raise it to weed out results whose colors turn dull.
The factor on hue differences (default 2). 1 equals OKLab; higher values penalize a change to another hue (skin → orange, blue → purple) more. 0 ignores hue.

pages.text:
The score on each candidate (0–100) is computed without AI as a weighted sum of score terms. Clean up and Auto optimize look for the settings with the highest score. The scoring rules and optimization budget are set per preset in 0. Optimize criteria, and each candidate is scored by the criteria of the preset that made it.
Score terms
Term What it measures Default weight
Fidelity How closely the result matches the background-removed source cells: (opacity mismatches + structure loss inside cells + color difference) ÷ samples. Structure loss is how far the source pixels inside a cell scatter from the cell average — large in cells that cut a sharp edge in half, regardless of the result color. A higher weight favors results that follow the source's colors and shapes more closely (smaller cells, more colors); a lower one favors simpler results. 4
Orphan pixels Share of orphan pixels with no same-colored pixel among their 8 neighbors (worst at 5% of opaque pixels). A higher weight favors clean results without specks, but penalizes art with many deliberate single dots such as pupils or sparkles. 1
Outline gaps Share of edge pixels that aren't outline (dark) colors. A higher weight favors results with an unbroken outline; set it to 0 for art drawn without outlines. 0.5
Color count How far the color count is from the target. Unlike the others, it multiplies the whole score down (see Target colors below). With the target color count on Auto this weight does nothing. 0.5
Frame consistency How differently colors are used between frames. Nothing to measure with a single frame; in an animation a higher weight favors results whose colors flicker less from frame to frame. 1
Grid fit How much the grid disagrees with color changes. The closer the cell lines sit between the source's color blocks, the better; a higher weight favors results whose cell size and lines match the source exactly. 2
1-px outline Share of outer outline pixels that are only 1 px thick; doubled bands of 2 px or more count against it. Measured on the final placed pixels at outline darkness 0.24 even if you lower it, so leaving black outlines uncounted earns nothing. 1-px lines running inward from the outline aren't doubling. Lower it if a thick outline is part of the style. 4
Major color shift How much a widely used source color (at least 1% of opaque pixels) turned into a different color as a whole (e.g. brown boots pulled toward gold). Measured with the scoring color distance (on the OKLab scale): up to 0.02 is fine; 0.10 is the worst. A higher weight favors results where large areas such as hair, clothes and boots keep their original hue. 2
Block repetition How much the result is still an enlarged image: the share of edge cells (judged by each cell's average source color) that sit in a same-color 2×2 block. Close to 1 when cells are half the real size or smaller and the result is needlessly large; dithering can't hide it. Up to 65% is fine; 95% is the worst. Lowering it penalizes results cut finer (larger) than the source cells less. 2
Among built-in presets, Faithful to source and Clean pixels use different weights (Built-in presets). Each term's value, badness % and weight for the selected candidate appear in the score breakdown under the preview and in the tile tooltip (Candidates and scores).
0. Optimize criteria
The settings column with 0. Optimize criteria expanded and the Optimize check in the 1. Background header
① 0. Optimize criteria · ② Optimize check
① 0. Optimize criteria is at the top of the settings column and is saved with the preset.
Setting Details
Trials The most settings Clean up and Auto optimize try (0–10000). 0 means no trial limit; whichever of trials and seconds is reached first stops the run. More trials make better settings more likely but take longer. Type a value or choose one from the right-click presets list. Settings without a preset start at 2000 trials.
Seconds The most time Clean up and Auto optimize spend on one preset (0–600 seconds). 0 means no time limit; with both trials and seconds at 0 it runs until it stops improving, and the cancel button stops it. Built-in presets start at 300 seconds (Quick check: 30), settings without a preset at 120 seconds.
Target colors · Auto · Strict If the result has more colors than the target, the whole score is multiplied by (1 − Color count weight × colors over ÷ target): with weight 0.5 and target 16, 20 colors lose 12.5% and 24 colors 25%. Auto (default) ignores the color count; Strict also penalizes fewer colors than the target by the difference.
Fidelity · Center weighted How Fidelity, the largest score term, measures the color difference between the result and the source, and how pixels inside a cell are weighted. Each value is explained in the How Fidelity compares table below.
Cell color · Group range Which color a source cell counts as when comparing cell by cell, and how close colors must be to form one group. Each value is explained in the Representative cell color table below.
Scoring color distance (major shift, cell match) The color distance used to compare candidates' scores. Separate from the palette's conversion color distance, it measures every candidate with the same ruler and is used only by Major color shift and cell-by-cell Fidelity. Each value is explained in the Choosing the scoring color distance table below.
Score weights (0 = ignore) Each score term's weight (0–10); 0 ignores that term. What each term measures, and which results win when you change its weight, is in the Score terms table above.
How Fidelity compares
The Fidelity box decides how Fidelity compares result pixels with the source. The same result can lose or keep points for dither patterns or stray dots inside an outline depending on this value. It is a scoring rule, so optimization never changes it.
Value How it compares Suits
Cell by cell Compares each result pixel with just its own source cell's color (see Representative cell color below) using the scoring color distance (default). Nothing is mixed with neighbors, so a stray colored dot inside an outline or a checkerboard dither pattern loses points cell by cell. Ordinary pixel-art characters where clean fills and outlines matter, and every cell must match its own source cell.
Blended with neighbors Converts the source cell averages and the result into light-linear lightness, red–green and blue–yellow channels, blurs lightness a little and color more with neighboring cells, and compares in OKLab (S-CIELAB style; always OKLab instead of the scoring distance). A dither pattern that blends into the source color from a distance counts as a match. Art that builds gradients with dithering, or has wide smooth areas such as skies and backgrounds; also for judging dithered results fairly.
Center weighted When on (default), pixels near the cell center weigh more when choosing the cell color (a pyramid that falls off toward the edges). Neighbor colors bleeding over the cell edge count less, so the cell color stays steady even when the source cells are slightly uneven. Off counts every pixel in the cell equally. Can be turned off for clean sources with little blur and exact cell edges.
Representative cell color
The Cell color box decides which single color a source cell counts as when comparing cell by cell. Source cells mix in blur, noise and neighboring fills, so the same result scores differently depending on what is taken as the cell's color. Used only with Cell by cell.
Six source cells that mix colors next to the same cells filled with their dominant-group and cell-average reference colors
From left: source cells (white lines = cell borders) · Dominant group (default) · Cell average — Cell average treats a cell that straddles two colors as a muddy in-between color that isn't in the source.
The cell split between outline and skin and the cell with outline bled into a corner become skin with Dominant group but a muddy brown with Cell average. So Dominant group accepts a result that paints that cell plain skin, while Cell average rewards a result that paints the muddy brown that isn't in the source. The plain skin cell is the same in both, so the choice only changes the score on cells that mix colors.
Value The source cell's color Suits
Dominant group Groups similar colors in the cell (within the group range) and takes the heaviest group's average (default). A few black outline pixels in the corner of a skin cell, or blurred edge colors, form small groups and drop out, so a result that paints the cell clean skin color counts as a match. Most AI pixel art with distinct outlines and fills.
Cell average Takes the average of every pixel in the cell. A cell an outline crosses gets a muddy mix of skin and black as its reference, so the result loses a little whether it paints that cell skin or black. Soft painting where colors really blend inside each cell (gradients, watercolor style), so no single group stands out.
Group range How different two colors can be and still form one group in Dominant group (OKLab distance, default 0.06). Smaller values split a single skin tone with JPEG noise into several groups, so the cell color wavers; larger values merge different fills such as skin and light shading. Optimize grid fit first's cell purity uses this value too. Raise it a little for noisy JPEGs; lower it a little for art with closely spaced shading steps.
Choosing the scoring color distance
A color distance is a ruler that turns how different two colors are into one number. The scoring color distance is used only for cell-by-cell Fidelity and Major color shift and never changes the result colors; it decides which differences count as worse mistakes among the same candidates. All three are on the OKLab scale, so the same thresholds apply (0.02 barely visible, 0.10 worst).
Three color strips from one skin color, changing only lightness, only chroma and only hue
From the top: lightness (L) — dark brown to pale skin · chroma (C) — grey to deep orange · hue (H) — one turn through the kinds of color at the same lightness and chroma. Each strip changes only that axis of one skin color.
OKLab and OKLCh are color spaces built so that differences match what the eye sees. OKLab places a color at lightness L and two color axes, a (green ↔ red) and b (blue ↔ yellow), and measures the difference as the straight distance between two points. OKLCh writes the same color as lightness L, chroma C (how vivid) and hue H (the kind of color), so you can see along which axis and how far a color moved, like the three strips above. The L·C·H weights of OKLCh hue-weighted multiply the differences on these three axes — raising H counts a change of kind of color (third strip) as bigger than a change of lightness only (first strip).
Apricot, gold, red, blue, grey and green gradients mapped to one 10-color palette with three color distances
From left: source gradients (top to bottom apricot, gold, red, blue, grey, green; lighter on the left) · OKLab · CIEDE2000 · OKLCh hue-weighted (default) — each pixel replaced by the nearest of the same 10 palette colors.
The scoring color distance measures the color difference between source and result with the same yardstick that picks the "nearest color" in this picture. Under OKLab, apricot in the middle of the grey strip and green where dark gold was count as close, so such a result loses little score; under CIEDE2000 and OKLCh hue-weighted they are a change to another color and are penalized heavily. So for pictures with many greys, metals or shadows, or where kinds of color must not mix, scoring with CIEDE2000 or OKLCh hue-weighted is safer (the distance that picks palette colors is set separately by the color distance in 6. Palette).
Distance How it measures Suits
OKLab OKLab is a color space built so that colors the same number apart look about equally different (perceptually uniform: around 0.02 is a barely visible difference whether the colors are dark or light, red or blue). This takes the straight (Euclidean) distance in it, weighing lightness, chroma and hue equally. Fastest and simplest. Images with few, clearly different colors, or when you want a neutral ruler that weighs no difference specially.
CIEDE2000 The industry-standard color difference formula (ΔE00) used in print and displays, measured in CIELAB (divided by 200 to match the OKLab scale). Differences the eye is dull to (chroma between very saturated colors) count less, sensitive ones (between near-grey colors) count more, and a correction for hue shifts around blue and purple is built in. Heavier to compute, so scoring gets a little slower. Art with many grey steps such as silver armor, grey stone or white clothes, or with lots of blue such as blue clothes or a night sky.
OKLCh hue-weighted Splits the OKLab difference into lightness (L), chroma (C, intensity) and hue (H, which color: red, yellow, blue and so on) and adds them with the L, C and H weights below (default 1 · 1 · 2, so hue counts double). The hue difference is scaled by chroma, so greys barely change and only a saturated color turning into another hue is penalized heavily. For example, a skin-colored hand turning red-cloth colored counts as a big mistake even at similar lightness. Characters where different hues of similar lightness touch, such as skin, a red shirt and orange hair; for weeding out results whose shading slips into a neighboring hue.
L weight The factor on lightness differences (0–1000, default 1). Raising it penalizes shading that became a step lighter or darker more; 0 ignores lightness. Used only with OKLCh hue-weighted; dimmed for the other distances. Raise it when the shading steps must stay exact.
C weight The factor on chroma differences (default 1). Raising it penalizes colors that faded (vivid red → dull red) or grew more intense; 0 ignores chroma. Raise it to weed out results whose colors turn dull.
H weight The factor on hue differences (default 2). 1 equals OKLab; higher values penalize a change to another hue (skin → orange, blue → purple) more. 0 ignores hue. Raise it to stop fills told apart only by hue (such as skin and red cloth) from merging.

pages.text:
Split a character into parts of different sizes, such as head, body and legs, draw them in each frame, and combine them into one frame to use as an animation while also exporting them as per-part sprites. You can draw several sets (skins) of body types, outfits or gear on the same part setup, swap between them, and swap them the same way in Unity.
The work follows the steps below. Each step is explained in detail on the pages in the right column.
Step What you do Details
1. Group Create a group layer that holds one character or one set of gear. You can also move layers you already drew into a group. Creating · Moving layers into and out of groups
2. Parts Add parts with their own size to the group and draw each part in every frame. Groups and parts · Drawing (part selected)
3. Layout Decide where each part sits in the frame: move it by hand, turn on auto layout, or place it differently in individual frames. Arranging (group selected) · Changing part positions per frame · Auto layout
4. Skins Draw another set of art for the same parts. A single part can also wear a different skin. Skins and slots · Empty skins and duplicating · Per-part choices and part-only skins
5. Outfits Choose the skin each group wears and save combinations you use often as outfit presets. Skin manager · Changing outfits and outfit presets
6. Export On save, produce the frame sheet, part atlas and Sprite Library assets for Unity. Export: frame sheet and part atlas · Exporting skins · Unity Sprite Library

When a normal layer becomes a part

pages.text:
You can turn a normal layer you already drew into a part, move a part to another group, or take a part out of its group as a normal layer. Each is a single undo step; it doesn't work on locked layers or locked groups, and a group can't go inside another group.
Dragging with Shift
Dragging the Body layer into the Props group with Shift held: highlighted destination group and blue insertion line
① Dragged layer · ② Blue line and highlighted destination group
While dragging ① a layer name in the timeline, hold Shift to move it into or out of a group instead of reordering. ② The blue line is the drop position and the highlighted name cell is the receiving group; a not-allowed cursor marks places you can't drop. Release Shift to go back to reordering. When the project has groups, the status bar shows this hint as you start dragging.
Drop on Result
Another group's row Puts it in as that group's top part. A collapsed group is expanded.
Upper or lower half of a part row in another group Puts it directly above or below that part.
A normal layer row, the upper half of its own group row, or outside all rows Takes the part out of the group as a normal layer.
When a normal layer becomes a part
The rectangle around the drawing in every frame (including pixels outside the canvas) becomes the part's size and position. The drawing stays at the same place on the canvas.
An empty layer, or one with an effect that draws without source pixels (such as Text), covers the whole canvas.
The drawing becomes the group's first-skin art and there is no 9-slice border. The layer's pivot (its default pivot and any per-frame pivots) is converted to be relative to the part, pointing at the same spot in the drawing.
When a part leaves its group
Only the art of the skin currently shown goes along. Art in other skins and the part's own part-only skins are removed, so if there is any, a confirmation (Other skins will be lost) appears first.
When taken out of a group, each frame's drawing stays where that frame's part position put it, and anything past the canvas becomes pixels outside the canvas. The part pivot becomes a canvas-relative layer pivot pointing at the same spot in the drawing, and frames that had their own position or pivot get their own pivot for that frame. The 9-slice border and per-frame positions are removed.
If an outfit preset gave that part its own skin, that entry is removed from the preset.

Parts can be dragged to reorder only within their own group. Dragging a group moves its parts with it.

Method Frames moved
Dragging or arrow keys in the group view, the part's right-click Position… Moves the base position, so every frame moves by the same amount. Per-frame differences are kept.

Per-frame distances are saved in the project file and the undo history, and survive the following edits.

Duplicating frames, Extend frames in the effects dialog Copied frames use the same positions as their source frames.
Duplicating a part layer The copied part gets the same per-frame distances.

Skin rules
Skins in the same group replace each other (swap).
② Different groups stack in layer order (overlay).
The artwork alone differs between skins. Parts, size, position, pivot and 9-slice are shared by all skins.
Skin names are unique within a group, including part-only skins.
Example: body, hair, armor
Put "hair" and "armor" groups above a "base body" group at the bottom; picking one skin in each group and stacking them makes one character. The gear groups' first skin, "none", is left empty and the gear is drawn in the other skins.
Group (bottom → top) Skins Purpose
Base body default · muscular · zombie Swaps the whole body.
Hair none · short · long Stacks on the body.
Armor none · leather · plate Stacks on top.
Creating skins
Create skins with New skin (empty) or Duplicate in the skin manager, or from the group's right-click Skin submenu. On a normal layer, right-click Add skin (turns into a group) creates the group and skin at once (Moving layers into and out of groups). A project with parts can produce two outputs on save; turn each on or off in ③ Output. Both come out as an image + Unity .meta.
The two outputs
① Frame sheet: an animation sheet with every layer composited in each frame. Group effects and per-frame part positions are included.
② Part atlas: one cell (sprite) per part × frame with content. If ④ the name is empty, it is <frame sheet name>_parts.
Part atlas sprites
A sprite's Pivot is the part pivot (or that frame's own pivot if it has one), and its Border is the part's 9-slice border.
Part effects are included in the sprites; group effects are not (Parts and layer effects).
Layout, sort order and cell names follow ⑤ the common sheet settings in the export dialog (Export). Old files that are no longer produced are moved to the app trash (see Files).

Turn on ① Sprite Library in the part atlas section of the export dialog to create a Sprite Library Asset for the Unity 2D Animation package per group × skin, named ② <part atlas name>_<group>@<skin>.spriteLib. Use them to swap a whole skin in Unity by changing one asset.
What a library contains
Category = part, Label = frame (0, 1 … or idle_0 …).
Libraries for the same group all share the same Categories and Labels; only the sprites differ. So one animation works for every skin.
A part/frame not drawn in a selected skin keeps its Category/Label but has an empty sprite entry; first-skin art is never substituted.
Using it in Unity
Put a Sprite Library component on the parent of each group's part objects and assign one of that group's libraries.
Give each part object a Sprite Resolver (Category = part) and keyframe its Label (frame).
To switch skins, just swap the asset on that group's Sprite Library component for another skin's.

pages.text:
AI chat is a window where you ask Claude Code or Codex CLI, installed on this computer, to look at the open image and edit it. The AI uses editor tools that Chickxel provides to place pixels, create frames, layers, parts and skins, add layer effects, and turn images made with Codex image generation into pixel art. No API key is needed; usage counts against your own Claude or ChatGPT subscription.
Category Pages
Getting started What it can do · One-time setup: install and log in · Opening the chat window · Claude and Codex tabs · How it works · Using other AI apps
Chatting Chatting · Progress display · Answering the AI's questions · Editing or deleting the last message · Continuing past chats · Help and example requests
Drawing and editing Edits the AI can make · Generate image → pixelate · Asking for layer effects · References: teach the AI your style
Safeguards Undoing · Limiting edits to the current file · Protecting locked layers
Troubleshooting Troubleshooting
How your work is protected
Undo: each AI reply is one undo step. Undo it all at once with Undo this step under the reply or Ctrl+Z (Undoing).
Locked layers: the AI never touches layers locked in the timeline (Protecting locked layers).
Current file only: when on, the AI edits only the image open when you send and can't open or create other files (Limiting edits to the current file).
Saving and tools: the AI saves only when asked, and runs with the CLI's built-in features such as shell commands turned off, using only Chickxel's tools. It searches the web only when you ask it to (How it works).
Asking the AI chat to "Add a 1px white outline to the character" and the outline appearing on the canvas

Chat with an AI inside the editor to create and edit images. Ask in plain words, like "add a black outline" or "draw 4 walking frames" (①), and the AI edits the open image directly (②).

No API key is needed. It uses Claude Code (Claude subscription login) or Codex CLI (ChatGPT subscription login) installed on your computer. Usage counts against each subscription. Pick which one to use with the ③ tabs at the top of the chat window.

pages.text:
The AI model isn't built into Chickxel. When you send a message, Chickxel starts the CLI on your computer, and the CLI talks to its company's model while calling editor tools through Chickxel's MCP server.
When you press Send, Chickxel starts Claude Code or Codex CLI (codex exec) and passes it your text and attached images.
The CLI sends the request to the Anthropic or OpenAI model with your signed-in subscription.
When the model calls a tool, the CLI sends an HTTP request to Chickxel's MCP server; the editor runs the tool and returns the result (text or an image). Each tool call appears as a tool line in the chat.
When the reply ends, everything changed in that turn is grouped into one undo step.
The MCP server and temporary MCP config
The first time you use an AI feature (AI chat, the AI Status window or the Effect Maker's AI pane), Chickxel opens an MCP server at an address reachable only from this computer (http://127.0.0.1:port/mcp, or localhost on Windows when that address can't be used). It picks a free port and creates a new random token each time the app starts; requests without the right token are rejected (HTTP 401).
The address and token are passed straight to the CLI as a temporary MCP config: Claude Code gets a config file in the temp folder (--mcp-config, --strict-mcp-config), and Codex CLI gets launch options (-c mcp_servers=…) with the token in an environment variable. This is separate from the MCP servers registered in your own Claude or Codex settings, so you don't need to register anything, and Chickxel doesn't change your settings. Temporary config files are deleted when the app closes.
If Allow external AI apps is on in Preferences > AI Status, Chickxel opens this MCP server as soon as it starts, and other AI apps can use the same editor tools with a token of their own (Using other AI apps).
What the AI can use
CLI Launch settings
Claude Code All built-in tools except web search and web fetch are turned off (--tools "WebSearch,WebFetch") and only Chickxel's MCP tools are allowed. The web tools are used only when you ask the AI to look something up (see Looking it up on the web under References). Other MCP servers from your settings aren't loaded.
Codex CLI Features such as the shell, the browser and image generation are turned off, and it runs in a read-only sandbox. Web search (web_search="live") stays on but is used only when you ask the AI to look something up. Chickxel's MCP tools are allowed without asking, and project documents such as AGENTS.md in the working folder aren't read.
Generate image → pixelate starts a separate Codex CLI with image generation turned on, only while it makes that image (web search off).
The AI pane of the Effect Maker window uses a different token and can only use tools that read the document and references, plus replacing that editor's source (web search off).
What is sent and what is stored
Your messages and attached images, and the images and document details the AI looks at with tools, go through the CLI to that company's model. When you ask for a web search, the search terms and the pages it reads go to that model too.
Chats are saved on this computer in a per-AI folder under <settings folder>/Chickxel/Chats/ (Continuing past chats).

Turning it on

With the install scripts, the path is %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Chickxel\Chickxel.exe on Windows and /Applications/Chickxel.app/Contents/MacOS/Chickxel.App on macOS. Copying it with ④ is more reliable than typing it. Where to paste it in each app:
App Where to register it
Claude Desktop Add the chickxel entry to mcpServers in claude_desktop_config.json, which Settings > Developer > Edit Config opens (Windows %APPDATA%\Claude\, macOS ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/), then quit Claude Desktop completely and start it again.
Claude Code Put the same JSON in .mcp.json in the project folder (it asks before using it the first time), or register it for every folder from a terminal with claude mcp add --scope user chickxel -- "path to the executable" --mcp.
Cursor Put the same JSON in ~/.cursor/mcp.json (all projects) or in the project's .cursor/mcp.json, and check that chickxel is enabled in the MCP list of Cursor's settings.
Codex CLI Instead of JSON, add [mcp_servers.chickxel] to ~/.codex/config.toml as below. Wrap a Windows path in single quotes (so TOML keeps the backslashes).
[mcp_servers.chickxel]
command = 'C:\Users\me\AppData\Local\Programs\Chickxel\Chickxel.exe'
args = ["--mcp"]
Once registered, the app lists the chickxel tools. Chickxel's drawing rules (look at the document first, coordinates, parts, how to use effects and so on) are passed along when it connects. Try asking the app something like "add a 1px white outline to the open image".
How it works
The AI app starts Chickxel --mcp. This process opens no window; it only passes messages between that app and the running Chickxel.
For each message, the bridge reads the Chickxel MCP server address (http://127.0.0.1:port/mcp) and the external connection token from mcp-external.json in the settings folder. The file exists only while the external AI connection is on.
Chickxel shows and runs only the allowed tools for requests with that token. Tools run in the editor, so the canvas changes right away, and the result (text or an image) goes back to the app.
Tools run in the order the app sends them. Long tools such as image generation send progress notes while you wait, and other requests are accepted meanwhile.
Because the bridge rereads the file for every message, you don't need to restart the app after restarting Chickxel. While Chickxel is closed, the app gets an explanatory error (see If it doesn't connect below).
Connection indicator
Right end of the status bar: the plug icon and
⑤ External AI connection indicator
⑤ While the external AI connection is on, a plug icon and a dim External AI show at the right end of the status bar. When another AI app calls a tool, it turns the accent color for 4 seconds with the tool's name (the picture is right after a draw_pixels call). It disappears when you turn the connection off.
Differences from AI chat
The editor tools are the same, but since the conversation happens in the other app, a few things differ.
Item AI chat External AI connection
Connection Chickxel starts the CLI and passes it a temporary MCP config. The app starts Chickxel --mcp. You register it in the app once.
Usage Your Claude or ChatGPT subscription (CLI sign-in) That app's account and plan, plus your Codex quota if image generation is on.
Undo One reply is one step (Undoing) One tool call is one step ("AI: tool name"). A request that called several tools takes several undos.
AI questions A question card above the input box (Answering the AI's questions) There is no ask_user; the AI asks in that app's conversation instead.
Opening files Opens files with open_file. Only with ② Allow opening files
Image generation Follows the drawing mode in drawing settings. Only with ③ Allow image generation. The subject image comes as a base64 PNG (subject_image) instead of an attached image number.
Current file only Turned on with the chat button (Limiting edits to the current file). Not used, whatever its state in AI chat.
Locked layers Never touched. The same.
Drawing rules Given as the system prompt. The same rules arrive as MCP instructions on connecting (some apps may not use them).
Where you see it Tool lines and result pictures in the chat window The app's conversation; Chickxel shows only the canvas changes and the ⑤ indicator.
Safety
The connection is open only on this computer (127.0.0.1), and only requests with the external connection token are accepted. The token is new each time Chickxel starts.
<settings folder>/Chickxel/mcp-external.json, which holds the token, exists only while the connection is on and is deleted when you turn it off or close Chickxel. Programs running under your account on this computer can read it and connect, so turn the connection off when you don't use it.
Opening files and image generation must be turned on separately, and external AIs never touch locked layers either. The rules tell the AI to save only when asked.
Images and document details the app looks at with tools go to that app's model, as described in that app's privacy information.
If it doesn't connect
Symptom Cause and fix
The app gets "Chickxel isn't running or its external AI connection is off" Start Chickxel and check that ① is on. The same happens if Chickxel quit unexpectedly; once it is running again, the app continues without a restart.
The app has no chickxel tools Check the config file's location and JSON (commas and brackets) and restart the app. The app starts the executable itself, so the path must point to the real file; if you moved Chickxel, copy it again with ④.
open_file or generate_pixel_art is missing or refused as "not available over the external AI connection" Turn on ② or ③ and reconnect so the app fetches the tool list again. ask_user is always left out for external connections.
Image generation fails with "Couldn't read subject_image as a PNG image" The subject image must be a base64 PNG without a data: prefix. If the app can't pass images that way, describe the subject in words instead.

Draw Paints blocks of pixels or single pixels, lines, rectangles, ellipses, fills, clears, and replaces colors. draw_pixels set_pixels draw_shape fill clear replace_color
Frames and animation Adds frames (optionally as copies) or deletes them, and sets frame durations and animation tags. Links cels across frames, unlinks them and recolors links. add_frame delete_frame set_frame_duration add_tag link_cels unlink_cels set_link_color
Layers Adds layers, changes their name, visibility, opacity, and pivot, and picks the frame and layer shown in the editor. add_layer set_layer set_current
Groups and parts Splits a character into parts such as head, body, and arms, and sets each part's position and size. add_group add_part set_part
Skins and outfits Creates alternative drawings of the same parts (such as clothes), switches between them, and saves or applies outfit presets. list_skins add_skin set_skin edit_skin list_outfits save_outfit apply_outfit
Layer effects Adds, changes, and removes layer effects that leave the drawing untouched, such as outlines, shadows, glow, hit flashes, shaking, and appear/disappear. When asked, it also applies them permanently or enlarges the canvas to fit them. list_effect_types get_effects add_effect set_effect remove_effect apply_effects expand_canvas_for_effects
Effect making Writes script effects (JavaScript) for looks the installed effects (the official effects and your packages) can't make and checks them on the preview chick. Saves a finished script as a personal script effect and opens it in the Effect Maker (you upload it yourself). While the Effect Maker is open it can read, rewrite and validate the source in its editor. get_script_api write_script_effect preview_effects save_script_effect list_script_effects get_script_effect_source get_effect_maker_source set_effect_maker_source check_effect_maker
Canvas and colors Changes the canvas size, the canvas (export) pivot and its representative layer, the palette colors, and the primary and secondary colors. resize_canvas set_canvas_pivot set_palette set_colors
Files Creates a new drawing, sets the temporary title of an unsaved new drawing, saves, and opens files (opening and creating are blocked while "Current file only" is on). new_project set_document_title save_project open_file
References Searches the images, notes and style rules in your reference folder and the user guide, saves the current drawing as a reference, and captions references. search_references get_reference get_style_rules add_reference set_reference_info
Other tools Asks you with a question card above the input box when a decision is needed. ask_user
Tool lines
The end of each ①② tool line shows in parentheses how long that tool took (e.g. get_image (22s), get_image (1m 20s)). For a failed tool it follows the error text, and it stays when you reopen the chat. A tool that is still running shows no time yet.
Linked cels
Ask AI 'link frames 4–8' or 'make that link green' to manage linked cels with link_cels, unlink_cels and set_link_color. get_document reports linked frames and colors per layer and group. Unlink results report both unlinked cels and effect end appearances baked into art.
Saving and temporary titles
It saves only when asked. If a never-saved new project has changes, it asks whether to save before switching to another document. When it draws on an unsaved new image that has no temporary title, the AI gives it a short title in your language (the title of new_project, or set_document_title — never for documents that have a file). It can change that image's temporary title even with Current file only on.

A turn where the AI added an outline effect, and the effect row in the timeline
① Effect row in the timeline (Outline) · ② Your request · ③ Tool line that added the effect (add_effect) · ④ Undo this step
The AI can use the same layer effects as the Effects dialog. Effects don't change the drawing's pixels, so you can still change or remove them later in the Effects dialog or the ① timeline.
Asking for an effect
② Ask things like "add a 1 px black outline to the character", "add a white hit flash on frames 3–4", "make it appear over the first 4 frames", or "put a shadow 2 px to the lower right".
Animated effects (hit flash, blink, shake, appear, and so on) play over the frame range you give. Without a range they cover the whole animation, as in the Effects dialog.
Effects are picked by ID (short IDs such as outline or hitflash; asset IDs for received effects and your own script effects) or by display name. The old built-in effect type IDs (chickxel.effect.outline and so on) still work and add the same official script effect (from the source built into the app if you deleted that official effect). Your own and received effect presets can be added by name too.
It can also change the settings, frame range, on/off state, order, and clipping of existing effects.
Applying effects permanently (baking them into the pixels) and enlarging the canvas to fit effects that spill outside it happen only when you ask.
Effect changes (③) are part of the AI's reply, so one undo step (④) undoes them too. Effects on locked layers are never changed.
Making new effects with scripts
When no installed effect can do it, the AI writes a script effect itself. For example: "Make an effect that flashes red and breaks into pieces when hit, as a script, and save it as my effect." These tools are in the Effect Maker group of the chat help.
get_script_api reads the script rules and API together. write_script_effect writes a script effect on a layer, and preview_effects shows the result. Scripts written by the AI run without asking, like source written on this computer (same sandbox and limits). If the source has an error, nothing is changed.
save_script_effect saves a layer's script effect as your own script effect and opens it in the Effect Maker window. list_script_effects and get_script_effect_source only read the list and source of your script effects.
get_effect_maker_source, set_effect_maker_source and check_effect_maker read, replace and check the editor source only while the Effect Maker window is open.
Without being asked, the AI adds useful settings on its own (anchor point, direction, speed, repeat, range, color, strength, size and so on) and briefly lists them in its reply. Effects that read another layer are built with a layer-picker setting. When it uses colors, it picks them per pixel by default so gradients work, and the results of check_effect_maker, write_script_effect and set_effect_maker_source may include a gradient hint (recommended).
Publishing is up to you; the AI can't publish effects online.

When something goes wrong, first press Check all again in the AI Status and Settings window. Each row shows whether installation, sign-in or the connection is the problem.
When the AI can't reach the editor
Codex tab: a red line explaining why the editor tools could not be reached, and an end line with only the time
① Red line with the likely reason · ② End line showing only the time (Codex)
If the AI CLI doesn't receive the tool list from Chickxel's MCP server, the chat shows a ① red line. It tells you, from the requests the server received, at which stage the connection stopped, and ends with the path of the CLI that tried to connect; compare it with the path in the AI Status window. When the MCP connection row in the AI Status window fails, it shows the same explanation plus the end of the CLI's error output.
Message Meaning What to check
No request arrived The CLI couldn't send a single request to Chickxel's internal server (the 127.0.0.1 address). Check whether proxy environment variables (HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY), a VPN or Windows security software block loopback connections on this PC.
The auth token did not match Requests arrived but the server rejected them because the token was wrong (HTTP 401). The authorization header in the temporary MCP config passed to the CLI wasn't applied. Update the CLI with Install or update and check again.
A request reached the server, but tools/list did not Authentication passed, but the connection stopped during initialization. Look at the HTTP stages and response codes under the message. GET: HTTP 405 is the normal answer because SSE isn't used, and even POST initialize: HTTP 200 doesn't mean the CLI accepted the initialization response. Try updating the CLI.
If requests arrived, the line below the message lists the server's recent requests with their stage and response code, like POST initialize: HTTP 200, GET: HTTP 405 (up to the last 8). Stages are request names such as POST initialize, POST notifications/initialized, POST tools/list and POST tools/call.
The editor connection uses a temporary MCP config that the app passes straight to the CLI each time it runs; it's separate from MCP servers registered in your own Claude settings. It's normal for your settings to have no chickxel server.
When the CLI path changes
If the CLI location changes during a chat (install or update, changing the executable), "The CLI path changed. Reconnecting the session; send your message again after the check." is shown instead of sending, and it checks again. Send your message again once the check is done.
What looks different with Codex
Codex replies appear all at once after they're fully written, and show only the ② time, not the cost (Claude shows the cost too).
If you distribute the app
If you distribute an app with this feature to others, check Anthropic's and OpenAI's usage policies (restrictions on using subscription logins in third-party apps).

To make a new language, export the translation CSV, add a language column, translate it and add the file back. Edit the CSV in a spreadsheet such as Excel or Google Sheets. You can add a partial translation; empty cells show English.
Exporting and translating
The Language part of the General tab in Preferences: the Display language list, the Export translation CSV…, Add language from CSV… and Open language folder buttons and the note
① Export translation CSV… · ② Add language from CSV…
Save a CSV file with ① Export translation CSV… in Preferences. You can open it in Excel, Google Sheets and so on.
The first row is key,ko,en and the second row is #name,한국어,English. Add a new column at the far right with the language code in the first row (e.g. ja) and the language name in the second row (e.g. 日本語).
Translate the text in that column. Braces such as {0} and {name} are placeholders for values, so keep them as they are (you may change their order).
CSV layout
Row Content
First row key and the language codes (key,ko,en,…). A language code uses letters, digits, - and _, up to 32 characters.
Second row #name and the name shown in the list for each language (#name,한국어,English,…)
Other rows The text key (<table>.<key>, e.g. UiStrings.Language_Label) and the text for each language. Don't change the keys.
The exported file is comma-separated UTF-8 (with BOM). Importing reads comma, semicolon and tab separators, so it's fine if Excel saves with semicolons because of your regional settings. One file can contain several language columns.
Adding and applying it
The Display language list open after adding a CSV with a Japanese column: 日本語 (ja) appears below 한국어 and English, with the import result below
③ The language added from the CSV (e.g. 日本語 (ja)); the number of imported strings is shown below the list
Choose the file with ② Add language from CSV… and it appears in the ③ language list. If you added just one new language, it is selected for you. Click OK and restart to apply it.
The number of strings added for each language appears below the list ("{name} ({code}): added {count} strings.").
Columns that aren't valid language codes are skipped and keys Chickxel doesn't have are ignored; the counts are reported.
Empty cells show the English text, so you can add your translation bit by bit. Adding the same language code again overwrites it. Added languages are saved as <settings folder>/Chickxel/Languages/<language code>.csv.
